reference.source: Williams Hematology / WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours
clinicalPearls: An aggressive neoplasm derived from plasmacytoid dendritic cell precursors, typically affecting older adults
Cutaneous lesions are the most common presenting feature, ranging from bruise-like plaques and nodules to widespread violaceous lesions
Bone marrow, blood and lymph node involvement frequently follow, and leukaemic dissemination is common
The defining immunophenotype is co-expression of CD4 and CD56 together with plasmacytoid dendritic cell markers such as CD123, TCL1 and CD303
The blasts are negative for lineage-specific myeloid and T/B markers, which helps distinguish it from acute myeloid leukaemia and lymphoblastic disease
There is an important association with, and risk of progression to, myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukaemia
CD123 is both a diagnostic marker and a therapeutic target, and central nervous system involvement should be considered given the aggressive behaviour
reference.pathophysiology: Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm is a clonal malignancy arising from precursors of plasmacytoid dendritic cells, the interferon-producing cells of the innate immune system. Malignant blasts overexpress the interleukin-3 receptor alpha chain (CD123) and retain markers of plasmacytoid dendritic cell lineage while co-expressing CD4 and CD56. Recurrent genetic lesions affect tumour suppressor and epigenetic regulatory genes, and there is molecular overlap with myeloid neoplasia that underlies the frequent association with myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia. The cells characteristically infiltrate the skin before or alongside spread to marrow, blood and lymphoid tissue.
additionalDifferentials: Acute myeloid leukaemia with cutaneous involvement (leukaemia cutis)
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with immunohistochemistry for CD4, CD56, CD123 and TCL1
Flow cytometry of blood and marrow for plasmacytoid dendritic cell markers
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to assess infiltration
Cerebrospinal fluid examination given central nervous system risk
Cytogenetic and molecular studies to detect associated myeloid abnormalities
Cross-sectional imaging for nodal and visceral involvement
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or ulcerating skin lesions with systemic symptoms
Cytopenias indicating marrow failure or evolving myeloid neoplasm
Neurological signs suggesting central nervous system involvement
Rising blast count signalling leukaemic transformation
reference.prognosis: The disease is aggressive with historically poor outcomes; targeted CD123-directed therapy and consolidation with allogeneic transplantation in eligible patients have improved responses, but relapse remains common.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing skin lesions as bruising, vasculitis or benign dermatosis and delaying biopsy
Confusing it with acute myeloid leukaemia without full plasmacytoid dendritic cell marker assessment
Neglecting central nervous system evaluation and prophylaxis
Overlooking an associated or evolving myeloid neoplasm
